paragraphs: The influence of the liberty of the press is not limited to political opinions. It reaches all the opinions of men, and it changes customs as well as laws. In another part of this work I shall try to determine how much influence the liberty of the press has had on civil society in the United States, to show what direction it has given to the ideas of the Anglo-Americans, and to describe the tone it has given to their character and feelings. For now, I intend only to examine the effects the liberty of the press has produced in the political world.

I confess that I do not have the firm and complete attachment to the liberty of the press that people feel for things that are supremely good in their very nature. I approve of it more because I remember the evils it prevents than because I weigh the advantages it secures.

If anyone could point out a middle position between the complete independence and the complete subjection of public expression of opinion, and one that could actually be held, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it. But the difficulty is to find such a position. Suppose you want to correct the abuses of an unlicensed press and restore the use of orderly language. You may begin by trying the offender before a jury. But if the jury acquits him, the opinion of a single individual becomes the opinion of the whole country. So too much has been done, and too little. If you go further, you must bring the offender before a court of permanent judges. But even there the case must be heard before it can be decided, and the very principles that no book would have dared to avow are proclaimed aloud in the pleadings. What was hinted at obscurely in a single work is then repeated in a multitude of other publications. The words in which a thought is expressed are only the body of the thought, not the idea itself. Tribunals may condemn the form, but the sense and spirit of the work are too subtle for their authority. Too much has been done to turn back, and too little to reach your goal, so you must go on. If you establish a censorship of the press, the public speaker will still be heard, and you have only made the mischief worse. The powers of thought do not depend, as physical strength does, on the number of their mechanical agents, and you cannot count a host of authors the way you count the troops of an army. On the contrary, the authority of a principle is often increased by how few men express it. The words of a strong-minded man, reaching into the passions of a listening assembly, have more power than the shouting of a thousand orators. And if free speech is allowed in any one public place, the result is the same as if it were allowed in every village. The liberty of speech must therefore be destroyed as well as the liberty of the press. That is the necessary end of your efforts. But if your aim was to repress the abuses of liberty, they have brought you to the feet of a despot. You have been driven from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without finding a single position along the way where you could take shelter or rest.

Some nations have special reasons for valuing the liberty of the press, apart from the general motives I have just pointed out. In certain countries that claim to enjoy the privileges of freedom, every individual agent of the government can violate the laws with impunity, because those he oppresses cannot prosecute him before the courts of justice. In that case the liberty of the press is not merely a guarantee of the citizens’ liberty and security. It is the only guarantee they possess. If the rulers of such nations proposed to abolish the independence of the press, the people would be justified in saying: Give us the right to prosecute your offenses before the ordinary tribunals, and perhaps we may then give up our right to appeal to the tribunal of public opinion.

But in countries where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people ostensibly prevails, the censorship of the press is not only dangerous but absurd. When the right of every citizen to share in governing society is acknowledged, every citizen must be presumed able to tell the different opinions of his contemporaries apart, and to weigh the different facts from which conclusions may be drawn. The sovereignty of the people and the liberty of the press may therefore be regarded as correlative institutions. In the same way, the censorship of the press and universal suffrage are two things that are irreconcilably opposed, and that cannot long be kept together among the institutions of the same people. Not one of the twelve million people who live in the territory of the United States has yet dared to propose any restriction on the liberty of the press. The first newspaper I looked at on arriving in America contained the following article:

In all this affair the language of Jackson has been that of a heartless despot, solely occupied with the preservation of his own authority. Ambition is his crime, and it will be his punishment too: intrigue is his native element, and intrigue will confound his tricks, and will deprive him of his power: he governs by means of corruption, and his immoral practices will redound to his shame and confusion. His conduct in the political arena has been that of a shameless and lawless gamester. He succeeded at the time, but the hour of retribution approaches, and he will be obliged to disgorge his winnings, to throw aside his false dice, and to end his days in some retirement, where he may curse his madness at his leisure; for repentance is a virtue with which his heart is likely to remain forever unacquainted.

Many people in France imagine that the virulence of the press comes from the uncertain social condition of the country, its political excitement, and the general sense of the evils that follow from them. They therefore suppose that once society has regained a certain calm, the press will give up its present vehemence. I am inclined to think that these causes explain the extraordinary ascendancy the press has gained over the nation, but that they have little influence on the tone of its language. The periodical press seems to me to be driven by passions and tendencies of its own, independent of the circumstances in which it is placed, and the present state of America confirms this view.

America is perhaps, at this moment, the country in the whole world with the fewest seeds of revolution. Yet the press there is no less destructive in its principles than in France, and it shows the same violence without the same grounds for indignation. In America, as in France, the press is a singular power, so strangely made up of good and evil that it is at once indispensable to the existence of freedom and almost incompatible with the maintenance of public order. Its power is certainly much greater in France than in the United States, though nothing is rarer in the United States than to hear of a prosecution brought against it. The reason is quite simple. Having once admitted the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, the Americans apply it with perfect consistency. They never intended to found a permanent state of things out of elements that change every day. So there is nothing criminal in attacking the existing laws, provided the attack does not involve a violent breach of them. They also believe that courts of justice are unable to check the abuses of the press. The subtlety of human language constantly escapes the severity of judicial analysis, and offenses of this kind tend to slip out of the hand that tries to seize them. They hold that to act effectively on the press, one would have to find a tribunal that was not only devoted to the existing order of things but also able to overcome the influence of public opinion. It would have to conduct its proceedings without publicity, pronounce its decrees without giving its reasons, and punish an author’s intentions even more than his language. Anyone who had the power to create and maintain such a tribunal would waste his time prosecuting the liberty of the press, for he would be the absolute master of the whole community, and he would be as free to get rid of the authors as of their writings. On this question, then, there is no middle ground between servitude and extreme license. To enjoy the priceless benefits that the liberty of the press secures, one must submit to the unavoidable evils it produces. To expect to gain the benefits and escape the evils is to cherish one of those illusions that commonly mislead nations in their times of sickness, when, tired of faction and worn out by effort, they try to combine hostile opinions and contrary principles on the same soil.
The small influence of the American journals can be attributed to several causes, among them the following.

The liberty of writing, like every other liberty, is most formidable when it is new. A people that has never been used to sharing in the conduct of State affairs places complete confidence in the first popular leader who catches its attention. The Anglo-Americans have enjoyed this liberty since the founding of the settlements. Besides, the press cannot create human passions by its own power, however skillfully it may kindle them where they already exist. In America politics are discussed with animation and a great variety of activity, but they rarely touch the deep passions that are stirred whenever the real interest of part of the community is harmed. And in the United States the interests of the community are in a most prosperous condition. A single glance at a French newspaper and an American one is enough to show the difference between the two nations on this point. In France the space given to commercial advertisements is very limited, and the news is not extensive, but the most essential part of the paper is the discussion of the politics of the day. In America, three-quarters of the enormous sheet laid before the reader are filled with advertisements, and the rest is often taken up with political news or trivial anecdotes. Only from time to time does one find a corner devoted to the kind of passionate discussion with which the journalists of France are accustomed to indulge their readers.

Observation has shown, and the natural shrewdness of the pettiest as well as the greatest despots has discovered, that the influence of a power grows in proportion as its direction is made more central. In France the press combines two kinds of centralization. Almost all its power is concentrated in the same place and held in the same hands, for its organs are far from numerous. The influence of a press organized in this way, acting on a skeptical nation, must be unbounded. It is an enemy with which a government may sign an occasional truce, but which it is hard to resist for any length of time.

Neither of these kinds of centralization exists in America. The United States has no metropolis. The intelligence and the power of the country are scattered widely, and instead of radiating from one point, they cross one another in every direction. The Americans have set up no central control over the expression of opinion, any more than over the conduct of business. These circumstances do not depend on human foresight. But it is thanks to the laws of the Union that no licenses are granted to printers, that no securities are demanded from editors as in France, and that there is no stamp duty, as there is in France and as there once was in England. As a result, nothing is easier than to start a newspaper, and a small number of readers is enough to cover the editor’s expenses.

The number of periodical and occasional publications in the United States is truly beyond belief. The best-informed Americans attribute the limited influence of the press to this excessive multiplication. It is accepted as an axiom of political science in that country that the only way to neutralize the effect of public journals is to multiply them without limit. I cannot understand why a truth so self-evident has not already been more widely accepted in Europe. It is understandable that people who hope to bring about revolutions by means of the press should want to confine its action to a few powerful organs. But it is quite incredible that the supporters of the existing state of things, the natural defenders of the law, should try to reduce the influence of the press by concentrating its authority. The governments of Europe seem to treat the press with the courtesy of the knights of old. They are eager to give it the same central power that they have found to be such a trusty weapon, so as to increase the glory of their resistance to its attacks.

In America there is hardly a hamlet that does not have its own newspaper. It is easy to see that neither discipline nor unity of purpose can be imposed on so scattered a host, and so each paper fights under its own banner. All the political journals of the United States are indeed lined up on the side of the administration or against it, but they attack and defend in a thousand different ways. They cannot succeed in forming those great currents of opinion that overwhelm the most solid obstacles. This division of the press’s influence produces a number of other consequences that are almost as remarkable. The ease with which journals can be started draws a multitude of people into them. But because the amount of competition rules out any considerable profit, the most distinguished classes of society are rarely drawn to these undertakings. Yet there are so many public prints that, even if they were a source of wealth, writers of ability could not be found to run them all. The journalists of the United States are usually in a very humble position, with little education and a vulgar turn of mind. The will of the majority is the most general of laws, and it establishes certain habits that form the characteristics of each particular class of society. In this way it dictates the etiquette practiced at courts and the etiquette of the bar. The French journalist is characterized by a violent, though often eloquent and lofty, manner of discussing the politics of the day, and exceptions to this habit are only occasional. The American journalist is characterized by an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace. He habitually abandons the principles of political science to attack the characters of individuals, to follow them into private life, and to expose all their weaknesses and faults.

Nothing can be more deplorable than this abuse of the powers of thought. I shall have occasion later to point out the influence of the newspapers on the taste and morality of the American people, but my present subject concerns only the political world. It cannot be denied that the effects of this extreme license of the press tend, indirectly, to maintain public order. People who already hold a high place in the esteem of their fellow citizens are afraid to write in the newspapers, and so they are deprived of the most powerful instrument they could use to stir up the passions of the multitude to their own advantage. *a

a [ They write in the papers only when they choose to address the people in their own name, as, for instance, when they are called on to repel slanderous charges and to correct a misstatement of facts.]

The personal opinions of the editors carry no weight at all in the eyes of the public. The only use of a journal is that it passes on knowledge of certain facts, and it is only by altering or distorting those facts that a journalist can do anything to support his own views.

But although the press is limited to these resources, its influence in America is immense. It is the power that drives the circulation of political life through every district of that vast territory. Its eye is always open to detect the secret springs of political designs and to summon the leaders of all parties before the bar of public opinion. It rallies the interests of the community around certain principles, and it draws up the creed that factions adopt. For it provides a means of communication between parties that hear and address one another without ever having been in direct contact. When a great number of the organs of the press take the same line, their influence becomes irresistible, and public opinion, when it is constantly attacked from the same side, eventually gives way. In the United States each separate journal has little authority, but the power of the periodical press is second only to that of the people. *b
b [ See Appendix, P.]
The opinions that take hold in the United States under the empire of the liberty of the press are often more firmly rooted than those formed elsewhere under the approval of a censor.

In the United States the democracy constantly raises new individuals to the conduct of public affairs, and so the measures of the administration are seldom governed by strict rules of consistency or order. But the general principles of the government are more stable, and the opinions most widespread in society are generally more durable than in many other countries. Once the Americans have taken up an idea, whether it is well founded or not, nothing is harder than to root it out of their minds. The same tenacity of opinion has been observed in England, where for the last century there has been more freedom of conscience, and more unshakable prejudice, than in all the other countries of Europe. I attribute this result to a cause that may at first sight seem to work in the opposite direction, namely the liberty of the press. Nations in which this liberty exists are as likely to cling to their opinions out of pride as out of conviction. They cherish them because they hold them to be just, and because they used their own free will in choosing them. They maintain them not only because they are true, but because they are their own. Several other reasons lead to the same result.

A man of genius once remarked that “ignorance lies at the two ends of knowledge.” It would perhaps have been more accurate to say that absolute convictions are found at the two extremes, and that doubt lies in the middle. For the human intellect may be considered in three distinct states, which often follow one another. A man believes without question, because he adopts a proposition without inquiry. He doubts as soon as he is confronted by the objections his inquiries may have raised. But he often succeeds in resolving these doubts, and then he begins to believe afresh. He no longer grasps a truth in its dimmest and most uncertain form. He sees it clearly before him, and he goes forward by the light it gives. *c
c [ It may, however, be doubted whether this rational and self-guiding conviction arouses as much fervor or enthusiastic devotion in men as their first dogmatic belief.]

When the liberty of the press acts on men in the first of these three states, it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing without question or investigation, but it constantly changes the objects of their instinctive convictions. The human mind continues to see only one point on the whole intellectual horizon, and that point is always moving. Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions, and of the misfortunes that are sure to befall those generations that abruptly adopt unconditional freedom of the press.

The circle of new ideas, however, is soon exhausted. Experience has touched them, and the doubt and mistrust that their uncertainty produces become universal. We may be sure that most people will either believe without knowing why, or will not know what to believe. Few can ever hope to reach that state of rational and independent conviction that true knowledge can produce in spite of the attacks of doubt.

It has been observed that in times of great religious fervor men sometimes change their religious opinions, whereas in times of general skepticism everyone clings to his own persuasion. The same thing happens in politics under the liberty of the press. In countries where all the theories of social science have been contested in turn, the citizens who have adopted one of them stick to it, not so much because they are sure of its excellence as because they are not convinced that any other is better. In the present age men are not very ready to die in defense of their opinions, but they are rarely inclined to change them. There are fewer martyrs, and also fewer apostates.

Another and still stronger reason can be given. When no abstract opinions are regarded as certain, men cling to the mere inclinations and outward interests of their position, which are naturally more tangible and more lasting than any opinions in the world.

It is not an easy question whether aristocracy or democracy is better fitted to govern a country. But it is certain that democracy annoys one part of the community and that aristocracy oppresses another. When the question is reduced to the simple form of a struggle between poverty and wealth, the tendency of each side becomes perfectly clear without further debate.
